title: Did God Choose Who Would Be Saved?
excerpt: Paul wrote that God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills, and Paul wrote that God desires all people to be saved. Five Christian traditions have tried to keep both sentences, and each of them is left with a question it can't fully answer.
body:
A woman is reading Romans aloud to a small group in her living room, a paragraph at a time, and she reaches the ninth chapter. "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" (Romans 9:13). She stops, and for a while nobody in the room says anything. A father has two grown sons who were raised at the same table and taken to the same church. One believes and one doesn't, and he has started to wonder whether the difference lies in the boys, in something he did, or in a decision made before either of them was born. And a skeptic who knows the Bible well has a charge that he thinks no Christian can escape. If God chose in advance who would be saved, then he made the rest for the fire and blames them for burning. If he wants everyone and fails to get them, then he is not God.

The skeptic's charge has two sides because the Bible has two sentences. The apostle Paul wrote both of them. "So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills" (Romans 9:18). And God "desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4). Most arguments about predestination are won by quoting one of those sentences and explaining the other away.

Another essay on this site tells [the history of the argument](/writing/did-god-choose-me-or-did-i-choose-god), from Augustine's quarrel with Pelagius to the friendship of Wesley and Whitefield, and it ends with a word for the reader who is afraid that she herself was not chosen. This one stays with the two sentences. It asks what each of them says where it stands, and what the great Christian traditions have done with both.

## Where All of Them Begin

The quarrel is narrower than its temper suggests. In the early fifth century a teacher named Pelagius held that a person can turn to God and obey him by the natural strength of the will. Augustine answered that the will itself is sick and has to be healed before it can turn. The church sided with Augustine, at Carthage in 418 and at Ephesus in 431, and a council at Orange in 529 added that even the first wish to believe is God's gift, while pronouncing a curse on anyone who taught that God foreordains people to evil.

Every tradition described below stands on that ground. Reformed, Wesleyan, Lutheran, Catholic and Orthodox Christians all say that grace comes first and that nobody is saved by his own effort. So the dispute is not over whether God's grace saves. It is over the question the council left alone. When the same grace is preached to two brothers and one receives it and the other doesn't, where does the difference come from?

## Romans 9, Read in Its Place

The chapter does not begin with a doctrine. It begins with a man in pain. "I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart," Paul writes, and he says he could wish himself "accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers" (Romans 9:2–3). His own people have, for the most part, not believed in their Messiah. The question on the table is whether God's promise to Israel has failed.

His answer is that God's choosing never ran along the lines people expected. Abraham had two sons, and the promise went through one. Isaac had twins, and before they were born God said the older would serve the younger. Then Paul quotes what God said to Moses: "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion" (Romans 9:15). In Exodus those words are spoken just after the golden calf, to a people who had earned nothing, and there they are an announcement of mercy. Paul draws from them the hardest sentence in the letter, that God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills.

He knows what he has said, because he raises the objection himself: "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?" (Romans 9:19). He does not answer it with an explanation. He answers with the potter: "Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use?" (Romans 9:21). Anyone who finds that reply hard has understood it.

The chapter does not stop there, and neither does the argument. When Paul asks why Israel missed what the Gentiles found, the reason he gives is a human one: "Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works" (Romans 9:32). In the next chapter God says of Israel, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people" (Romans 10:21). In the chapter after that the branches are said to have been "broken off because of their unbelief," and Paul adds that "if they do not continue in their unbelief," they "will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again" (Romans 11:20, 23). Readers on every side have also noticed a difference in the way Paul speaks of the two kinds of vessel. The vessels of mercy are those God "has prepared beforehand for glory." The vessels of wrath are only said to be "prepared for destruction" (Romans 9:22–23), and God is described as bearing with them "with much patience."

So the same three chapters hold the strongest statement of God's freedom in the New Testament and some of its plainest statements that people are lost through their own unbelief and that the way back stands open. Paul sets these beside each other and does not explain how they fit.

Christians have read the chapter in three main ways, as the Study Bible's notes on this site set out. One reading, Augustine's and later the Reformed churches', takes Paul to be speaking of God's choice of individual persons for salvation. A second, common among Wesleyans, takes the choice to rest on God's foreknowledge of faith. This is close to the reading the Greek-speaking church had long held. John Chrysostom, preaching on this chapter late in the fourth century, called the choice of Jacob "a sign of foreknowledge," and said of the vessels of mercy that Paul "does not mean that all is God's doing. Since if this were so, there were nothing to hinder all men from being saved." A third reading holds that Paul's subject is peoples and their place in history, Israel and the nations, and that individuals share in election by belonging to Christ.

## 1 Timothy 2:4, Read in Its Place

The other sentence is also part of an argument. Paul is telling a church how to pray. He asks for prayers "for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions" (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and the kings in question were pagans. His reason is the character of God, who desires all people to be saved. He grounds that in the creed: "there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all" (1 Timothy 2:5–6). One God made everyone, one mediator died for all, and so the church's prayers may not stop at the edge of its own membership.

The plain sense is that God wants every human being saved. The difficulty is as plain: not every human being is. Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, listed three ways Christians had tried to hold those together.

The first is Augustine's. In a handbook written late in his life he took the verse to mean "that no man is saved unless God wills his salvation: not that there is no man whose salvation He does not will, but that no man is saved apart from His will." The second, which Augustine also offered, reads "all" as all kinds: in Aquinas's words, "some men of every class and condition." The third came from the East. John of Damascus, in the eighth century, wrote that "God's original wish was that all should be saved and come to His Kingdom," and he called that God's antecedent will. What God wills in view of a person's refusal he called the consequent will. Aquinas gave the picture of a judge who "antecedently" wills "all men to live; but consequently wills the murderer to be hanged."

The first two readings make the verse say less than it seems to, and many Reformed teachers have been uneasy with them. They prefer to say that God truly desires what he has not decreed, and that we are not shown how. The third keeps the verse at full strength. It then has to explain the sentences in Romans 9.

## Five Accounts in Their Own Words

The Reformed churches gave their answer at the Synod of Dort in 1619 and in the Westminster Confession of 1646. God chose his people, Westminster says, "without any foresight of faith or good works," out of "his mere free grace and love." The rest he was pleased "to pass by, and to ordain them to dishonor and wrath for their sin." The last three words carry weight. In the Reformed account election is unearned, but condemnation is always earned. Dort says that those who are passed by are left "in the common misery into which they have wilfully plunged themselves," and that this teaching "by no means makes God the author of sin (the very thought of which is blasphemy)." What the Reformed are guarding is grace. If God chose me because of something he saw in me, then that something, and not his mercy, is the reason I am saved.

The Arminian answer was written in 1610 by the followers of Jacobus Arminius, and John Wesley's heirs hold it in substance. God determined from eternity "to save in Christ, for Christ's sake, and through Christ, those who, through the grace of the Holy Ghost, shall believe on this his son Jesus." The choice is real and eternal, and it is a choice of believers. The same articles say that a person "can of and by himself neither think, will, nor do any thing that is truly good," so that faith itself is impossible without grace. But of that grace they say, "it is not irresistible." What the Arminian is guarding is the character of God. If the invitation goes to everyone, then God means it for everyone.

The Lutheran churches answered in 1577, and their answer is the hardest to place on anyone else's map. Election, they say, "extends only over the godly," and it is "not to be investigated in the secret counsel of God, but to be sought in the Word of God." They reject as false the teaching "that God is unwilling that every one should be saved." In the same list they reject the teaching that there is "in us" a "cause of God's election." If a person is saved, it is wholly God's doing. If he is lost, it is wholly his own. Asked why, then, one and not another, the Lutheran confession declines to answer, and says the question comes from reason and not from the gospel.

The Catholic Church spoke at the Council of Trent. It condemned the claim that those who are not saved are "by the divine power, predestined unto evil." It also condemned the claim that the human will, when God moves and calls it, "cannot refuse its consent, if it would." Aquinas, whom Catholic teachers still follow closely, says without flinching that "God does reprobate some," but he defines the word with care. Reprobation is "the will to permit a person to fall into sin, and to impose the punishment of damnation on account of that sin." Within those limits Rome has allowed more than one school to teach.

The Orthodox churches never made Augustine their chief teacher. John of Damascus states their starting point: "while God knows all things beforehand, yet He does not predetermine all things." A council of Eastern bishops at Jerusalem in 1672, answering a Calvinist confession that had appeared under a patriarch's name, said that God predestined some to glory "since He foreknew the one would make a right use of their free-will, and the other a wrong," that grace goes before everyone as a light, and that God "equally wills the salvation of all, since there is no respect of persons with Him."

## The Question Each One Is Asked

None of the five gets through both sentences untroubled.

The Reformed Christian is asked about 1 Timothy 2:4, and about the father's second son. If God passes by, what does it mean to say that he desires that son's salvation, and can the invitation the son hears on Sunday be sincere? The Reformed answer that it is sincere, that no one who comes is turned away, and that the two wills of God meet somewhere we can't see.

The Arminian and the Orthodox Christian are asked about Romans 9. Paul says the choice was made when the twins "had done nothing either good or bad," and "not because of works" (Romans 9:11). The objection he expects, that no one can resist God's will, is not one anybody would raise against a choice based on foreseen faith. And if grace is given alike to two brothers, and one believes, the difference lies in the brother. They answer that faith is the opposite of a work, the empty hand, and that no beggar boasts of having held his hand out.

The Lutheran is told that he has stopped halfway, and that a position which affirms both ends and denies the line between them is a refusal to think. He answers that Scripture stops there too.

The Catholic is asked by Protestants whether a grace that waits on our cooperation is still grace alone. He answers that the cooperation is itself the work of grace in a will set free.

## What We Have Done With It

Paul had a use for this doctrine, and it was not ours. When he was afraid in Corinth, the Lord told him to keep speaking, "for I have many in this city who are my people" (Acts 18:10). He wrote from prison, "I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus" (2 Timothy 2:10). Election, for him, was the reason to keep going in a hard city. It never told him whom to give up on.

We have used it to stop. We have looked at a neighbor, or a whole people, and decided that the matter was closed. We have told grieving parents things about their children that no confession on any side permits anyone to say. And those of us who hold the other view have done our own harm with it. We have laid a son's unbelief entirely on his own choosing or on his parents' failures, as though the Bible had never said that faith is a gift.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

All five traditions confess that salvation is by grace from first to last, and that Pelagius was wrong. All five confess that God is not the author of sin and that no one is condemned except for his own sin. Westminster says "for their sin," and Jerusalem, Trent and the Lutherans say the same in their own ways. All five preach the gospel to every person as an invitation that is meant.

How God's choosing and a person's believing fit together is a question of the second order. The creeds don't address it. Churches that share every line of the creeds have answered it differently for fifteen hundred years, and this essay does not choose among them.

What no tradition claims is a list. Nobody has been shown who is chosen, and nothing in any of these confessions tells the father which of his sons stands where.

He might notice what the doctrine did to the man who taught it. The apostle who wrote that God hardens whom he wills began that chapter by saying he would give up his own place in Christ if it would bring his kinsmen in. He ended the argument two chapters later with a door still open: "God has the power to graft them in again." Whatever Paul knew about election, it left him in anguish for the people outside and still praying for them. The father has been told the same two things and no third. God is free in his mercy, and God wants his son.

*"So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills."* (Romans 9:18)

*"This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth."* (1 Timothy 2:3–4)
